intro/hello: This lecture is about the step that turns a language model into an assistant: fine-tuning.
intro/base: Pretraining gives us a base model, one that has read a large slice of the web and can continue any text.
intro/more: But ask it a question, and it may simply write more questions, because on the web, questions often come in lists.
intro/doc: It is not broken. It is doing exactly what it was trained to do: continue the document.
intro/sft: The first half of this lecture is supervised fine-tuning: training on written-out examples of the behavior we want.
intro/answer: Afterwards, the same question gets an answer, and the model stops when it is done.
intro/cost: The second half is about cost. Updating every weight of a large model is expensive, so we will learn Laura, which trains a small low-rank correction instead.
intro/next: And all of it is the starting point for learning from rewards instead of examples.
sft/what: Supervised fine-tuning, or S F T, starts from demonstrations: prompts, each paired with the answer we wish the model had given.
sft/loss: Training uses the very same loss as pretraining, the negative log-probability of each next token, but now on the answers.
sft/step: So nothing about the machinery is new. Only the data changed.
sft/sources: Demonstrations come from people writing answers, from old datasets rephrased as instructions, from stronger models, and from real conversations.
sft/igpt: For InstructGPT, in twenty twenty-two, labelers wrote answers for about thirteen thousand prompts.
sft/pref: After that fine-tuning, plus the feedback training of later chapters, labelers preferred its one point three billion parameter model to the hundred and seventy five billion parameter G P T three it started from.
sft/lima: And the Leema paper found that just one thousand carefully chosen examples made a capable assistant.
sft/hyp: Its authors’ explanation: the knowledge comes from pretraining, and fine-tuning mostly teaches the format to use it in.
template/roles: A conversation is a list of messages, each with a role: system, user, or assistant.
template/flat: But the model reads one flat sequence of tokens. A chat template is the rule that flattens the conversation.
template/special: It marks where each message starts, who wrote it, and where it ends, using special tokens that no typed text can produce.
template/chatml: In the chat M L format, each message opens with im-start, then the role, and closes with im-end.
template/gen: At inference time, the server writes the conversation so far, plus the opening of an assistant message, and lets the model continue.
template/stop: Generation ends when the model writes the end token itself. So the model must learn to produce it, or it will ramble on.
template/same: And a model must be served with the same template it was trained on. A different one is a pattern it has never seen.
mask/same: Rendered through the template, a conversation is ready for the pretraining loss: at every position, predict the next token.
mask/not: But we do not want the model to get good at writing everything here: not the system prompt, and not the user’s questions.
mask/mask: So each position gets a mask, m. One for tokens the assistant wrote, zero for everything else.
mask/end: The end-of-turn token counts as the assistant’s too. That is how the model learns to stop.
mask/read: Masked-out tokens stay in the context. The model reads them; its predictions there are just never graded.
mask/loss: The loss multiplies each token’s log-probability by its mask, and adds them up...
mask/avg: then divides by the number of ones: an average over the answer tokens only.
mask/count: In this two-turn conversation, ten of the fifty tokens carry loss.
mask/torch: In pie torch, the masked targets are usually set to minus one hundred, a value the cross-entropy function skips.
toy/setup: Here is the whole recipe on a model small enough to see completely: under four thousand weights, and a forty-word vocabulary.
toy/web: Its web is six hundred made-up pages: lists of facts, quiz pages full of questions, and a few question-and-answer pages.
toy/base: Ask the base model a bare question, and it writes the next quiz question. It learned that from the quiz pages.
toy/chat: Give it the chat template, and it stumbles: it has never seen these tokens.
toy/demos: Now fine-tune on sixteen short conversations, with loss on the answers only.
toy/curve: The loss on the demonstrations, in red, collapses within a hundred steps.
toy/answers: And the chat prompts now get answers, each followed by the end token.
toy/knew: The model already knew every capital from the fact pages. The demonstrations only taught it where to put the answer, and when to stop.
forget/purple: But watch the purple curve: the loss on held-out web text. While the red one falls, it climbs.
forget/broken: And the bare question now gets nonsense. The model is forgetting the web.
forget/name: This is catastrophic forgetting: a network trained on new data loses what it learned from old data.
forget/why: The loss only measures the new batch, so gradient descent has no reason to preserve anything else.
forget/shared: And every weight is shared, so the weights that held the old skill get bent toward the new one.
forget/gentle: The first remedy is to be gentle: a smaller learning rate, and fewer passes over the data.
forget/replay: The second is replay: mix some old data into every batch, so the old loss keeps being optimized.
forget/flat: With half of each batch from the web, the purple curve stays nearly flat, and the bare question keeps its old answer.
forget/others: Other remedies penalize moving away from the starting weights, or train far fewer of them. That second idea leads to Laura.
cost/full: Everything so far was full fine-tuning: every weight gets a gradient and an update.
cost/bytes: With Adam in mixed precision, each parameter costs about sixteen bytes.
cost/wg: Two for the weight in B float sixteen, two for its gradient...
cost/ma: four for a thirty-two-bit master copy, and eight for the two running averages of Adam.
cost/total: For a seven billion parameter model, that is about a hundred and eight gigabytes before activations: more than an eighty gigabyte G P U holds.
cost/copy: And every fine-tune produces a whole new copy of the model: thirteen and a half gigabytes, per task, per customer.
cost/peft: Parameter-efficient methods freeze the pretrained weights and train something small instead. The one that won is Laura.
rank/idea: Write the fine-tuned weights as the old ones plus a change: W nought plus delta W.
rank/simple: Full fine-tuning learns every entry of delta W. But what if the change is simple, made of only a few directions?
rank/r1: The simplest matrix is rank one: a column times a row. Every row is a multiple of the same row.
rank/rankr: A rank r matrix is a sum of r such pieces, and it can be stored as a tall, thin B times a short, wide A.
rank/cost: That takes r times d plus k numbers, instead of d times k. For a four-thousand-wide matrix at rank eight: sixty-five thousand, instead of sixteen million.
rank/svd: The singular value decomposition takes any matrix apart into rank-one pieces, sorted from strongest to weakest.
rank/best: Keep the first r, and you have the best rank r approximation there is. Eckart and Young proved that in nineteen thirty-six.
rank/grow: Watch the rank grow. This matrix is built like a fine-tuning update: a few strong directions, plus a little noise.
rank/small: By rank four or five, the error is already small.
rank/noise: Random noise is different. Its singular values are all alike, and every dropped piece costs as much as the last.
rank/evidence: Fine-tuning updates look like the first kind. Pretraining already built the features; adapting mostly turns a few of them up or down.
lora/what: Low-Rank Adaptation, Laura, from twenty twenty-one, builds the low-rank idea into the model.
lora/freeze: Pick a weight matrix, W nought, and freeze it. It gets no gradient, and no optimizer state.
lora/path: Beside it, add a second path: A squeezes the input down to r numbers, and B spreads them back out.
lora/h: The two outputs are added, with the update scaled by alpha over r.
lora/count: Only A and B train: at rank eight, about four tenths of one percent of the matrix.
lora/gpt3: On G P T three, this cut the trainable parameters about ten-thousand-fold, and each checkpoint from three hundred and fifty gigabytes to about thirty-five megabytes.
lora/zero: Now the clever detail: B starts at zero. Then B times A is zero, and step zero is exactly the pretrained model.
lora/whyA: Why not A too? Look at the gradients. The gradient of B passes through A, so it is not zero.
lora/stuck: The gradient of A passes through B, so at first it is zero. B moves, then A follows. If both started at zero, neither would ever move.
lora/alpha: And alpha over r keeps the size of the update steady as you change the rank, so r can be turned without re-tuning everything else.
lora/typical: Typical settings are ranks from eight to sixty-four, with alpha equal to r, or twice r.
merge/which: Which matrices get adapters? A transformer block has the attention projections, for query, key, value and output, and the matrices of the M L P.
merge/paper: The original paper adapted attention only, and found that query and value together beat spending the whole budget on one matrix.
merge/all: The cue Laura paper later found that matching full fine-tuning needed an adapter on every linear layer. That is the usual default now.
merge/merge: After training, the adapter folds into the weights: W nought, plus alpha over r times B A. Same shape, same speed.
merge/latency: That is what set Laura apart from earlier adapter layers, which added extra steps to every forward pass.
merge/many: Or keep adapters separate: one base model in memory, and a small adapter chosen per request.
merge/size: A rank-eight adapter on query and value of a seven billion parameter model is about eight megabytes, against thirteen and a half gigabytes for a full copy.
merge/swap: And subtracting the update restores the original, so even merged adapters can be swapped.
qlora/still: Laura removes the gradients and optimizer state of the base, but the base weights still sit in memory, two bytes each.
qlora/qlora: cue Laura, from twenty twenty-three, stores the frozen base in four bits, and trains sixteen-bit adapters on top.
qlora/dequant: Each block of weights is decoded back to sixteen bits on the fly, used, and thrown away. Only the storage is four-bit.
qlora/block: To quantize, take a block of sixty-four weights and divide by the largest, so everything lands between minus one and one...
qlora/snap: then snap each weight to the nearest of sixteen levels, and store that level’s number: four bits.
qlora/nf4: Which sixteen levels? Trained weights are spread like a bell curve, crowded near zero. N F four puts its levels at quantiles of a normal distribution: dense where the weights are.
qlora/even: Evenly spaced levels waste codes on the thin tails. On these weights, the error of N F four is about fifteen percent lower.
qlora/dq: Each block also stores its scale, adding half a bit per weight. Double quantization compresses the scales too, down to about an eighth of a bit.
qlora/paged: And paged optimizers move optimizer state out to C P U memory during spikes, instead of crashing.
qlora/mem: Together: a seventy billion parameter model needs about eleven hundred gigabytes to fully fine-tune, about a hundred and forty with Laura, and under forty with cue Laura.
qlora/one: The paper fine-tuned a sixty-five billion parameter model on a single G P U with forty-eight gigabytes.
distill/cost: Human-written demonstrations are the expensive part. A cheaper writer is another model.
distill/seq: In sequence-level distillation, a strong teacher answers many prompts, and a small student is fine-tuned on those answers.
distill/examples: Alpaca did this with fifty-two thousand answers from an Open A I model. DeepSeek’s small reasoning models came from about eight hundred thousand samples of R one, with no reinforcement learning at all.
distill/soft: With the teacher’s weights in hand, the student can learn more: at every position, the teacher’s whole probability distribution.
distill/kl: The loss becomes a K L divergence from teacher to student, with the same answer mask.
distill/dark: A sampled word says only: this one. The distribution also says which wrong answers were plausible. Hinton called that dark knowledge.
distill/race: Train two students on the same teacher: the one learning from samples keeps jittering, while the one learning from probabilities converges smoothly.
distill/limits: The limits: a student inherits its teacher’s mistakes, and imitators copy style far more easily than ability.
outro/sft: To recap. A base model continues documents. Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations teaches it to write an assistant’s reply, in a template, ending when it should.
outro/mask: The loss is masked to the assistant’s tokens. And narrow fine-tuning forgets, unless you replay old data or change less.
outro/lora: Laura freezes the weights and learns a low-rank update, B times A, with B starting at zero, and folds back in for free.
outro/qlora: cue Laura stores the frozen base in four-bit N F four, putting large fine-tunes on a single G P U.
outro/distill: And distillation lets a stronger model write the demonstrations.
outro/next: One idea runs through all of it: imitation can only be as good as its examples. Going beyond them takes a different signal, a reward that says which answer is better.
